summary: A 1970 note proposing a third-level protocol called the Logger Protocol, by four authors. Third-level protocols sit above the basic host-to-host rules and define higher-level services, in this case apparently for logging in.

plainLanguage.summary: The Logger Protocol describes how a user at one host could connect a teletype to another host's monitor. Two logger programs set up the link, then sender and receiver programs carry the conversation.

questions: how do you log in to a remote arpanet host
why use ascii for teletype communication
how does the logger protocol establish a connection
subtitle: A proposed way to connect a user's teletype to a foreign host monitor.

tldr.problem: A user needs a network convention for connecting a local teletype to a foreign host's monitor.
tldr.mechanism: A send-logger and receive-logger establish a full-duplex link; sender and receiver programs then pass teletype input and monitor output.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes conventions for setup, character coding, break handling and input transmission, while leaving program implementation to each site.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 56 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text presents a proposed third-level protocol and says implementations are installation-dependent.

sections.title: Four Programs for Remote Terminal Access
sections.content:
The proposal describes four programs: a send-logger and receive-logger to establish a full-duplex link, then a sender and receiver to pass data between the user's teletype and the foreign monitor. After setup, the loggers leave the conversation to the sender and receiver.

The RFC says the programs' exact implementation depends on each installation. It proposes that the receive-logger listen as user zero on socket zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Two logger programs arrange a two-way connection. After that, a sender and receiver pass the user's typing and the foreign monitor's replies.

sections.title: Setting Up and Closing the Link
sections.content:
The send-logger connects to user zero, socket zero at the foreign host. If the receive-logger can accept the request, it closes that initial link, chooses a pair of sockets and connects back; the send-logger and receive-logger then complete the two-way connection and activate the data handlers.

When the user finishes, the sender closes both links. The RFC says it would be desirable for the receiving NCP to tell its receiver about the closure so it can log the user off and free resources.
sections.plainLanguage: The loggers first check that the remote side can accept the user, then establish the two-way connection. When the user finishes, the sender closes the links.

sections.title: Character Codes and Break Characters
sections.content:
The proposal recommends 128-character USASCII for communication between a teletype and a foreign monitor. A host using another internal code can translate to and from ASCII in its sender and receiver.

The RFC distinguishes a break used as an immediate panic command from a break used to leave a subsystem after current work finishes. It proposes using the INT control command for the panic function and mapping a seldom-used local character to the foreign system's exit character when necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts use USASCII for the teletype conversation and translate when their internal code differs. The proposal separates an immediate interrupt from an orderly exit and allows local characters to be mapped to those actions.

sections.title: Sending Input and Echoing Characters
sections.content:
The user can choose to send several command lines in one message, send at each carriage return, or transmit character by character. The user should be able to change modes, and the receiving program must buffer data into a form accepted by its monitor.

The RFC recommends that the local host echo typed characters and that the foreign machine suppress its own echo, if it can.
sections.plainLanguage: The user can send input in groups, at each carriage return or one character at a time. The local host should show typed characters so the remote host does not need to echo them.
